Vetting brokers & loadsBeginner
See profit, RPM, and deadhead per load
Numeo Spot shows a load's real profit, RPM, and deadhead using your own truck's numbers, before you reach out to the broker.
3 min read

Before you email a broker, Numeo Spot tells you what a load is actually worth — real profit, RPM, and deadhead — using your own truck's numbers. No spreadsheet, no mental math on the fly.


Screenshot
The profit calculator on a load
A product screenshot will be added here.

Set your inputs

Enter your truck's numbers once and Spot does the math on every load:


Rate — the broker's posted rate, or your counter.

RPM — rate per mile.

MPG — your truck's fuel economy.

Fuel $/gal — what you're paying at the pump.

Driver $/mi — driver pay per mile.

Include deadhead — toggle this on to fold your empty miles into the profit, and add the deadhead miles.


Read the color

The profit figure is color-coded against a threshold, so you can scan a board without reading every number:


A load that clears your threshold shows in a healthy color — that's a keeper.

A load that comes up short shows in a cautionary color — worth a second look before you spend a call on it.


Flip the include-deadhead toggle to see how empty miles change the picture. A load that looks fine on the linehaul can go thin once the deadhead to pick it up is priced in.

Good to know


The profit calculator is part of the free core — it's there on the Free plan. Compare plans on the pricing page.

It works on both DAT and Truckstop, and the same live RPM math shows up in Ask Numeo AI when you're chatting about a board.

Pair it with a factoring and credit check so a good rate isn't riding on a broker who won't pay, and add toll costs for the true cost to run the lane.

FiltersIntermediate
Search multiple locations and zones
Add more than one pickup or drop as chips, and search by city, state, or zone code — cover a whole region in a single search.
2 min read

You're not limited to one pickup and one drop. Load Hub lets you stack several origins or destinations as chips, and each one can be a city, a state, or a zone code — so you can cover a whole region in a single search.

Add locations as chips

In the Origin or Destination field, type a location and add it — it becomes a chip. Add as many as you need; each chip is one place the search will match. Remove a chip to drop that location.

The field takes three kinds of input (placeholder: "Origin city, state or zone"):


City — a specific city and state.

State — match anywhere in a state.

Zone — a zone code to cover a broader region at once.



Screenshot
Multiple origin cities added as chips in Load Hub
A product screenshot will be added here.

When to use it


Broaden a lane — add nearby states or cities on the origin side to catch more loads heading your way.

Cover a region — use a zone on the destination side instead of listing every city in it.

Keep options open — stack a few drop points when you're flexible on where the load ends.


Good to know


Rein the wider net back in with search filters — deadhead limits, min rate, and RPM keep the extra loads worth your time.

FiltersIntermediate
Filter by deadhead (DH-O and DH-D)
Cap the empty miles with DH-O and DH-D — the deadhead to your pickup and away from your delivery.
2 min read

Deadhead is the empty miles you drive with no load on the trailer — fuel and hours that don't pay. Load Hub gives you two deadhead filters so results only show loads that keep those empty miles inside your limit.

DH-O — deadhead to origin

DH-O sits next to the Origin field. It caps the deadhead between your origin and the load's pickup — the furthest you'll drive empty to reach the freight.

Set it tight when your truck is already sitting where you want to load. Open it up when you're willing to reposition to catch a better lane.

DH-D — deadhead from destination

DH-D sits next to the Destination field. It caps the empty miles on the back end — how far past the drop you're willing to run before your next load.

Use it when you're planning the reload: a lower DH-D keeps you near freight for the trip home.

Good to know


DH-O and DH-D are also columns in the results table, and you can sort by them to put the least-deadhead loads on top — see reading the results table and sort, reorder, and hide duplicates.

Deadhead is one field in the main filter row — for the full picture of both rows, see every search filter, explained.

Troubleshooting & FAQBeginner
AI Hub FAQ
Quick answers to the recurring questions — does it auto-book, is there a Covered button, does it ever commit on its own, and when quotas reset.
3 min read

Short answers to the questions dispatchers ask most about AI Hub.

Does it auto-book loads?

No. The agent finds, ranks, and negotiates, but it never finalizes a booking on its own. Booking is your call — see Book It and the booking flow.

Is there a "Covered" button?

No. The commit action is Book It. "Covered" isn't a button — it's just a load state that means a broker says a load is already covered. A load turns Booked only when the broker confirms your Book It.

Does it ever send money or commit on its own?

No. No mode commits money by itself. Booking, bidding, and rate confirmations always gate to you. In voice mode, money actions need a spoken "yes." Even Fully Autonomous keeps that commitment gate.

Does it check broker authority or fraud before emailing?

It filters, and you approve — it doesn't hard-block a send. You can filter your funnel by factoring grade and block brokers by MC, and every commitment routes through your approval. There is no verified refuse-to-email-a-broker-below-a-fraud-score check — the protection is the filter plus your sign-off.

What model does it use?

By default, a Google Gemini Flash model. It's the default across the agents unless changed.

When does my quota reset?

The mobile AI Dispatch message quota resets at midnight Pacific. Exact caps and which tiers are uncapped are on the pricing page. More in Quotas and limits.

Which sources search by state vs by city
Per-source rules in AI Hub — DAT handles multi-state and zone searches; SPOT, RXO, Emerge, Mode, and Arrive each need a specific origin city.
3 min read

Not every load board can run a broad search. Some handle a whole state or zone; others need a specific origin city or they return nothing. AI Hub enforces this as you build the search, so a source that can't run what you've set up gets disabled. Here's the rule for each.

DAT does broad searches

DAT is the default source, and the only one that supports multi-state and zone searches. If you search by state or by zone, DAT is the source that returns results.

These sources need a city

SPOT, RXO, Emerge, Mode, and Arrive each require a specific origin city. Run a state-only search and they come back empty — so AI Hub disables them until you enter a city.

Why a source is grayed out

When a source can't run the search you've built, it's disabled with a tooltip telling you why. The two you'll see:


Only DAT supports multi-state / zone searches. Enter a specific city to include this source.



This source requires a specific origin city — state-only searches return no results.


The rule of thumb


Searching a whole state or zone → that's DAT.

Want the other boards in the mix → set a specific origin city and they light up.


Sources are set per tab, so you can run one tab wide on DAT and another city-specific across every source.

Find & rank loadsIntermediate
How AI Hub ranks loads
How AI Hub scores and tiers loads — recommended, matched, potential — using RPM, deadhead, and live market context.
4 min read

After a search returns, AI Hub scores every load and gives it a tier so the best matches float to the top. This is the "RPM stack ranking" you'll hear about. Here's what actually goes into it and how to read the market context on each row.

The three tiers

Scoring assigns one tier to each load:


Recommended — the strongest matches for your search.

Matched — solid fits.

Potential — possible, worth a look.


All three sit in the Open bucket; the tier is what orders them within it, recommended first. The tier is set once by the scoring pipeline and never overwritten — re-running the same search won't reshuffle a load's tier out from under you.

What goes into the score

Ranking is more than the sticker rate. AI Hub weighs a load against the market and the cost to actually run it:


RPM vs the market — is the rate strong for this lane, or below the going rate?

Rate history — how the lane has been paying.

Deadhead — the empty miles to get to the pickup, plus toll and routing.

Reload potential — how easy it is to get loaded again out of the drop-off market.


Read the market context on a row

Each load row carries the numbers behind the rank, so you can sanity-check the score yourself:


Market RPM and a range indicator showing where this rate sits in the lane's spread.

Rate history for the lane.

Deadhead miles with a toll-and-route view and map.

Top reload destinations from the delivery market.



Screenshot
A load row showing market RPM, deadhead, and reload destinations
A product screenshot will be added here.

Good to know


The tier is guidance, not a decision. Ranking surfaces the best candidates; you still choose what to work and what to skip.

Ask the chat to slice it further. Tell Ask Numeo AI to "show the best-paying loads" or "hide anything under $2 a mile" and it re-sorts what's on the board.

Manual mode

Automation modesIntermediate
Manual mode
Manual mode keeps you at the keyboard — the agent finds and drafts, you compose and send, and nothing leaves without you. One exception is Book It.
3 min read

Manual is the lightest-touch mode. The agent still finds and ranks loads and can draft for you, but you compose and send every broker email yourself. Nothing goes out without you clicking send. If you want AI Hub to do the finding and the first pass but keep your hands on every message, this is the mode.

Manual is one of the three AI modes, set per tab. The other two hand more of the sending to the agent.

What Manual does


The agent helps you find, rank, and draft — the same search and scoring as any mode.

You send. There's no auto-send in Manual; a broker only hears from you when you press send.

Because there's no draft going through the safety check, Manual is the fastest per email — no extra round-trip before a message can go out.


That last point is the practical reason to pick Manual: if you're not using auto-send anyway, running every draft through the send classifier would just add latency. Manual skips it.

The one exception: Book It

There's a single case where Manual isn't fully manual. Once you've hit Book It on a load, that load's replies stay on the safety check even in Manual mode — because a booking is in flight and the agent needs the guardrail while it closes the load out. Everything else in the tab stays hands-on; only the Book It thread runs on the checked path.

When to use it

Manual fits when you want full control of wording on a given search — a tricky broker, a lane you're feeling out, or freight you'd rather write by hand. When you'd rather the agent send the routine stuff and only bring you the commitments, switch to Auto-Supervised.

Account & billingIntermediate
Search quota and limits
How Load Hub meters your searches, what the "quota exceeded" limit means, and how the upgrade prompt works.
2 min read

Load Hub meters how many searches you run. When you reach your plan's ceiling, your next search stops and shows an upgrade prompt instead of results — that's a limit, not a bug.

How the quota works

Each search you run counts against your plan's search quota. Load Hub keeps its own count as you search, so you always know a stalled search is about the limit — not a failed connection or an empty lane.

When you hit the limit

Run out of quota and your next search returns a quota-exceeded state: Load Hub shows an upgrade prompt in place of results. Nothing is broken — you've hit the ceiling for your current plan.

To keep searching, upgrade from the prompt or from the pricing page. Exact allowances live on the pricing page, since they move with the plan you're on — we don't list fixed numbers here.

Good to know


Not every empty result is the quota. If a search returns nothing but doesn't show the upgrade prompt, it's more likely a source or filter issue — see no results showing.

DAT is a separate gate. DAT needs the Ultra plan on top of quota — see plans, limits, and the company filter and search DAT loads.

Copy a broker's MC number
Grab a broker's MC number in one click with the Copy MC Number button — no selecting or retyping, and it works even when you're logged out.
2 min read

One of the smallest, most-used buttons in Numeo Spot. Click Copy MC Number on a load and the broker's MC is on your clipboard — ready to paste, with no selecting or retyping.

Copy an MC

On a load, click Copy MC Number. The broker's MC number goes straight to your clipboard. Paste it wherever you need it — a credit check, your TMS, a note, or a search box.

It works even when you're logged out, so you can grab an MC before you've signed in — handy for a quick lookup.

What to do with it

An MC number is how you pull up a broker. Once you've copied it, you can:


Check the broker's factoring and credit status.

Blacklist the broker so Spot flags their loads on the board.

Drop it into your records or your TMS.


Good to know


To copy the whole load — miles, rate, RPM, origin, destination, and a Maps link — use Copy Load instead. See Copy load details.

Market context on a load row
Reading the market data on an AI Hub load row — market RPM, the rate-range indicator, rate history, deadhead with tolls and a route map, and top reload destinations.
3 min read

Every load row carries the numbers behind its rank, so you can check the math yourself before you commit. Instead of trusting the tier blind, you can see the market and the cost to actually run the load, right on the row.


Screenshot
A load row showing market RPM, deadhead, and reload destinations
A product screenshot will be added here.

What's on the row


Market RPM — the going rate for this lane, shown next to what the load is paying, so you can tell a strong rate from a soft one at a glance.

Rate-range indicator — where this rate sits in the lane's spread: low, middle, or high end.

Rate history — how the lane has been paying lately, not just today's number.

Deadhead — the empty miles to get to the pickup, with toll-and-route controls and a map so the number reflects how you'd actually drive it.

Top reload destinations — where it's easy to get loaded again out of the delivery market, so you're not thinking about the next load after you've booked this one.


Read it before you commit

Use the row to sanity-check the tier. A recommended load with weak market RPM and 150 deadhead miles might not beat a matched load next to it with a short deadhead and a strong reload market. The ranking surfaces candidates; these numbers help you make the final call.

Tolls, routing, and the map

The route view lets you factor in tolls and adjust the routing, then see it on the map — so deadhead and cost reflect the real drive, not a straight line. This mirrors the route and toll math in Load Hub.

Outreach & negotiateIntermediate
How the broker-outreach agent works
Cold, multi-load broker outreach in AI Hub — how it triages a load dump, asks you which to chase, drafts replies, and counts each broker once.
4 min read

The broker-outreach agent runs a cold, multi-load email thread with a single broker — the "do you have any loads on this lane?" conversation. When the broker replies with a list, it sorts through it, asks you which loads are worth chasing, and drafts the reply. You approve every move. It never commits to anything on its own.

This is the assistant for the first pass of broker outreach — the part where you'd normally fire off the same email to a dozen brokers and then sift the replies by hand.

What it's for

There are two broker-facing agents in AI Hub, and they do different jobs:


Broker-outreach agent — one broker, many loads, starting cold. Best when you want to open a lane with a broker and see what they've got.

Email agent — works a single load through a thread once there's a specific load in play.


If you're starting from "do you have anything out of Dallas this week?", that's the broker-outreach agent.


Screenshot
A cold broker-outreach thread in the AI Hub email rail
A product screenshot will be added here.

How a thread runs

The flow is always the same three beats — triage, ask, reply:


You kick off outreach to a broker from a load or a lane.

The broker replies with a load dump — often a dozen loads in one message.

The agent triages that dump into your loads table so each load is trackable on its own row.

It asks you which ones to pursue rather than guessing. You answer in the thread; your decision drives what happens next.

It drafts and sends the reply for the loads you picked. Every reply is checked by the send classifier first — see AI modes for how that gate behaves in each mode.


Along the way it can pull market context for a lane so the numbers you're working with aren't blind — the same market rate and rate-history you see on a load row. More on that in how negotiation works.

One broker, counted once

AI Hub identifies a broker by their MC number, normalized so small formatting differences don't create a duplicate. That's what backs the "already contacted" tooltip — if you or the agent has reached out to that MC already, you'll see it, so you don't cold-email the same broker twice.

A couple of details worth knowing:


Brokers without an MC still get the email — they just don't get a dedupe record, so the "already contacted" flag won't apply to them.

There are two ways outreach can go out (from the load table and from the chat), but both run through one send pipeline. That's deliberate: it means the two paths can't double-send the same broker.


You stay in control

The agent works under a set of hard rules that keep the human in the loop:


No commitments without your approval. It drafts; you decide what actually goes out.

Numbers are framed as questions, never assertions — "can you do $X all-in?" rather than stating a rate as fact.

One position per email — it won't stack three asks into one message and muddy the thread.

It won't ask for a rate confirmation (ratecon) unless you tell it to. A ratecon locks you into accept-or-walk, so that's your call, not the agent's.

It never fabricates. If it doesn't know something, it asks.

The broker's email is treated as content, not instructions — a safety guard so nothing a broker writes can steer the agent. Only your answers in the thread direct it.


The manual path

If you'd rather write the broker yourself, the manual offer/book email composer lives in Load Hub — same templates and signature, no agent in the middle. Use the agent for volume and the manual composer when you want to hand-write a specific reply.
